title: Was Mesopotamia the Cradle of Civilization?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether Mesopotamia was the cradle of civilization. They define civilization as structure (class hierarchy, rulers often religious, laws, permanent settlement, trade and commerce) as opposed to culture as behavior, and trace the Neolithic Revolution and agriculture roughly eleven thousand years ago. They cover Mesopotamian firsts: writing on clay tablets that began as accounting and tax records, Gilgamesh as possibly the first literary work, organized religion, the calendar and timekeeping, science and art. They weigh rival early settlements such as Caral-like sites in China along the Yellow River, Catalhoyuk in southern Turkey, and Gonur Depe in Turkmenistan, and discuss Jared Diamond's view that agriculture was a mistake, along with disease and war as costs of civilization. The episode closes with Patrick McGovern's theory that alcohol drove the start of farming, with evidence of fermented fruit and rice beverages in China and beer residue in Gonur Depe pottery. The final listener mail is a story about a sailor's supposed encounter with a cargo cult, which the hosts treat as likely fake.

segments.title: Opening banter and the question
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the question of whether Mesopotamia was the cradle of civilization and joke about hunter-gatherer life and the thirty-person band limit.

segments.title: Defining civilization and the Neolithic Revolution
segments.summary: They describe the shift to agriculture about eleven thousand years ago and define civilization as structure: class hierarchy, rulers, laws, settled life, religion, and trade.

segments.title: Was agriculture a mistake and the rise of science
segments.summary: Chuck cites Jared Diamond's argument that agriculture was a mistake, and they discuss how surplus labor by others freed a ruling class to develop science, math, calendars and astronomy.

segments.title: Mesopotamian firsts: Sumer, writing and Gilgamesh
segments.summary: They introduce Mesopotamia and Sumer, then discuss the invention of writing on clay tablets for tax and accounting records, the move to phonetic writing, and Gilgamesh as possibly the first literary work.

segments.title: Religion, calendars, art and the costs of civilization
segments.summary: They discuss organized religion and priestly control, the Babylonian calendar and timekeeping, early art, and downsides such as war, slavery and epidemics.

segments.title: Competing early settlements
segments.summary: They weigh other Neolithic sites, including Yellow River settlements, Catalhoyuk in southern Turkey, and Gonur Depe in Turkmenistan, and whether those lacked social hierarchy or simply haven't been found to have one.

segments.title: Alcohol as the reason for farming
segments.summary: They present Patrick McGovern's hypothesis that the desire for alcohol drove the start of agriculture, and the debate over whether beer or bread came first.

segments.title: Ancient beer and fermentation in China and Mesopotamia
segments.summary: They describe the Neolithic Chinese fermented rice and fruit beverage made with saliva, McGovern's pottery residue analysis including tartaric acid and beer contaminants, and the Sumerian goddess of beer and her beer recipe on tablets.

segments.title: Listener mail: the castaway and the cargo cult
segments.summary: A listener's story of a solo sailor who washed ashore on a South Pacific island and was treated as a god by a cargo cult that used leftover World War Two items. The hosts doubt it is true.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and invite listeners to send mail to the show.
